problems.title: Bond-enthalpy estimate versus experimental combustion enthalpy of ethyne

Question 23 (Local Section Exam, multiple choice).

The standard enthalpy of combustion of ethyne can be estimated from the tabulated bond dissociation enthalpies (BDE) shown below to be $-982\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. The experimental $\Delta H^\circ_{\mathrm{combustion}}$ is $-1256\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Which is the best explanation for the discrepancy?

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\textbf{Bond} & \textbf{BDE}\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) \\
\hline
\ce{C#C} & 839 \\
\hline
\ce{C-H} & 412 \\
\hline
\ce{O=O} & 498 \\
\hline
\ce{C=O} & 741 \\
\hline
\ce{O-H} & 463 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

$$\ce{C2H2(g) + 2.5 O2(g) -> 2 CO2(g) + H2O(g)} \qquad \Delta H^\circ_{\mathrm{expt}} = -1256\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$$

(A) The tabulated $\ce{C-H}$ BDE does not account for the unusual strength of the bond formed to the $\textit{sp}$-hybridized carbon in $\ce{C2H2}$.
(B) The tabulated $\ce{O=O}$ BDE does not account for the unusual weakness of the bond in dioxygen due to its paramagnetism.
(C) The tabulated $\ce{C=O}$ BDE does not account for the stabilization due to electronic delocalization in carbon dioxide.
(D) The tabulated $\ce{O-H}$ BDE does not account for the stabilization due to hydrogen bonding in water.

In contrast, compounds $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ react with $\ce{KOH}$ in DMSO to give not only $(E)$- and $(Z)$-2-pentene but also another alkene $\mathbf{D}$.

a. Draw structures for compounds $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{D}$, clearly indicating stereochemistry if applicable.

b. What is the relationship (constitutional isomers, enantiomers, diastereomers, or not isomers) between compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$?

c. What is the relationship (constitutional isomers, enantiomers, diastereomers, or not isomers) between compounds $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$?

d. $(E)$-2-pentene has a melting point of $-140\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and a normal boiling point of $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, while $(Z)$-2-pentene has a melting point of $-180\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and a boiling point of $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Explain why the $(E)$ isomer has a significantly higher melting point, but essentially the same boiling point, as the $(Z)$ isomer.

e. No alkenes with the formula $\ce{C5H10}$ are chiral. Draw the structure of a chiral alkene with the formula $\ce{C6H12}$.
